Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Palais Lascaris, Nice, France - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)

Coordinates: 43.6967, 7.2716

Orientation: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, home to a remarkable collection of ancient musical instruments. Encounter the exquisite craftsmanship of the Harpe by Naderman, Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, Violes gambe by William Turner, and Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore. Delve into the evolution of musical expression through these meticulously crafted instruments, each with its own unique history and significance. Uncover how these exquisite pieces showcase the artistry and innovation of instrument makers throughout history, shaping the way we experience music today. Discover the rediscovered Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) and the distinctive maker's mark on the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581) as you journey through this musical tour. Your first stop is Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780). Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris in Nice and let your eyes wander over the intricate carvings and gilded embellishments. From this vantage point, you'll appreciate the delicately painted floral motifs and the acoustic engineering that made this instrument a marvel of its time.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a renowned luthier based in Paris, crafted the harp before you. Naderman used carved, painted, and gilded wood, employing a traditional single-action pedal and crochet mechanism, which allowed musicians to alter string length by a semitone. This innovation enabled more complex compositions and nuanced performances, cementing his reputation in the realm of French musical instruments. The harp was initially owned by the Viscountess of Beaumont, integrating it into the elegant social circles of 18th-century France. In 1995, the harp was rediscovered in the attic of the Château de Busset in France, long after it had fallen into obscurity. Its revival led to the City of Nice acquiring it in 2007, ensuring its preservation and subsequent display at the Musée du Palais Lascaris. This acquisition placed the harp among the second most significant collection of musical instruments in France, right after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris. François fought to preserve his father's designs while advancing harp craftsmanship, influencing the next generation of musicians. Now housed among over 500 instruments, the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) stands as an emblem of both artistic beauty and technological advancement at a time when the French court reveled in opulence.

Directions: Continue through Palais Lascaris — next is Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581).Stop 2: Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581)

Coordinates: 43.6967, 7.2716

Orientation: Stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581.

In the late 16th century, Anton Schnitzer, a master craftsman from Nuremberg, produced this tenor sackbut, known today as one of the earliest surviving examples of its kind in original condition. Schnitzer's distinct maker's mark and the year of production, 1581, are inscribed on the bell rim, bearing testimony to his expertise in brass instrument making. This act preserved the piece for future generations. In 2001, the sackbut found a new home at the Palais Lascaris, a venue dedicated to celebrating the history of musical instruments. This relocation enabled the sackbut to be displayed in a setting that honors its craftsmanship and historical significance. Its presence here offers a tangible link to the period when brass instruments like the sackbut bridged medieval music with the Renaissance tide, paving the way for modern trombones. Reflecting on the harp from earlier in your visit, consider how string instruments evolved alongside these brass giants, shaping the contours of musical history.

Directions: Next: Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652).

Stop 3: Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652)

Coordinates: 43.6967, 7.2716

Orientation: As you approach William Turner's viola da gamba, crafted in London in 1652, notice how the light catches its original carved head and pegbox, reflecting its nearly untouched state over the centuries.

In 1652, the English luthier William Turner crafted a six-string bass viola da gamba in his workshop located near Aldgate. Unlike many other viols from the 17th century that were later modified into cellos, this particular bass viol remained largely in its original condition, preserving its original carved head and pegbox. Antoine Gautier, a dedicated Niçois amateur musician and avid collector, bequeathed the viol to the public collections of Nice, the city where he was born, in 1904, allowing it to become a cherished part of the Palais Lascaris. The instrument is not merely a static display piece; it is maintained in playable condition and has been used for live concert performances in the palace's salons, keeping its rich sound alive for modern audiences. Now imagine what innovation came next — the viols and violins crafted by Italian artisans known for their unparalleled craftsmanship.

Directions: Your final stop in Palais Lascaris: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696).

Stop 4: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696)

Coordinates: 43.6967, 7.2716

Orientation: Stand directly before the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, Milano, 1717. Notice the instrument’s elegant proportions and robust form, hinting at the rich sound it would have produced, larger than that of the violes gambe by Turner you saw earlier.

By September 1904, the city officially accepted Gautier's bequest, marking the beginning of its long journey through various local institutions. Paolo Antonio Testore, who crafted this petite basse de violon in Milan in 1717, followed in the prestigious footsteps of his father Carlo Giuseppe Testore, producing instruments that exemplified Italian string mastery. The Testore family's commitment to quality is evident in the instrument's design, renowned for its durability and rich tonal quality, which were essential features in earlier orchestral developments.

That's 4 stops — Basse de violon crafted by Paolo Antonio Testore in Milan in 1717 and Harpe rediscovered in the attic of Château de Busset in 1995.
